topic: 限时听力：多人讨论与观点
grammarFocus: 转折、让步、同意与不同意；转述观点。
title: Week 39 Listening: Timed Multi-Person Discussions and Opinions
instructions: 本材料为模拟练习，不是官方雅思考试，也不对应任何官方分数。本材料仅包含听力部分，共四个部分、40道题。请先听录音（或由他人朗读），再作答；题目顺序与录音顺序一致。所有填空题答案必须逐字来自原文，且不超过字数限制。选择题请选择最符合原文的选项。判断题请选择 True、False 或 Not Given；选择 Not Given 时，说明所缺信息。
transcript:
Section 1: Social Dialogue

M: Hi, is this the right room for the repair café? I saw a poster in the library.
W: Yes, come in. Welcome. I’m one of the volunteers. What have you brought?
M: A kettle. It just stopped heating. I thought about buying a new one, but they’re not cheap, and it seems a waste.
W: Absolutely. Let’s have a look. Could you put it on the table? … Right. First thing, is it still under guarantee?
M: No, I’ve had it about three years.
W: That’s fine. We can still open it. Do you mind if I ask you to help? We like people to see how it’s done.
M: Sure, though I should warn you I’m not very practical.
W: That’s what most people say. Don’t worry. So, the first step is to unplug it—always unplug. Then we take off the base. There are three screws here. Can you see them?
M: Yes, I think so. Do you want me to undo them?
W: If you would. … Good. Now, the most common problem with kettles is the switch or the element. In your case, I suspect the switch. Look at this little metal strip—it’s bent.
M: Is that why it doesn’t work?
W: Probably. It’s not making contact. We can bend it back, but it may fail again. Alternatively, we can replace the switch. We keep a few spare parts.
M: How much would a new switch cost?
W: About four pounds. Much less than a new kettle.
M: Let’s do that, then. Actually—wait. Is it safe? I mean, with electricity…
W: Good question. We only do this with the kettle unplugged, and we test everything before you take it home. I’m not a qualified electrician, but I’ve been doing this for years, and we have a checklist. If I’m not sure, I ask one of the other volunteers. There’s a retired electrician here today, actually.
M: That’s reassuring. And the repair is free?
W: The repair is free. We ask for a donation if you can afford it—it helps with parts and insurance—but there’s no obligation.
M: Of course. I’ll definitely donate. So how long will it take?
W: About twenty minutes. While you wait, would you like a cup of tea? There’s a table over there.
M: That would be great. Thanks. Actually, can I ask—do you fix other things? I’ve got a lamp at home that flickers.
W: Bring it next month. We’re here on the first Saturday of every month. Lamps are usually easy.
M: Perfect. I’ll do that.

Section 2: Social Monologue

W: Good evening, everyone, and thank you for coming to the community meeting. I’m Priya, and I coordinate the local repair café network. I’ve been asked to give a short update on how things are going and what we need.

First, the good news. In the last twelve months, our five cafés have repaired just over nine hundred items. That’s up from about six hundred the year before. The most common items are kettles, lamps, vacuum cleaners, bicycles and clothing. We’ve also started a small tool-lending service, which has been surprisingly popular.

Second, the less good news. We are struggling to find volunteers with electrical skills. We have plenty of people who can sew or fix bicycles, but only three volunteers across the whole network are confident with electrical repairs. That limits how many items we can accept. If you know anyone—a retired electrician, an engineer, even a confident hobbyist—please put them in touch with me.

Third, funding. Our main costs are insurance, spare parts and room hire. This year we received a small grant from the council, which covered insurance, but that grant is not guaranteed next year. We’re asking for donations from visitors, and most people are generous, but it’s not enough to plan ahead. So we’re setting up a monthly giving scheme—five pounds a month from regular supporters. If fifty people sign up, that would cover our basic costs.

Fourth, and this is important, we want to reach areas we haven’t reached yet. At the moment, most of our visitors come from the wealthier side of town. That’s not surprising—people need time and confidence to come along—but it means we may be missing the people who would benefit most. We’re planning two pilot sessions in the east of the city, working with a community centre there. We’ll need volunteers willing to travel.

Finally, a date for your diary. Our next training session for new volunteers is on the fourteenth of next month, from ten until one. It’s free, and lunch is provided. You don’t need to be an expert; you just need to be patient and willing to learn. Thank you.

Section 3: Academic Discussion

Tutor: So, we’ve been looking at the evidence on hybrid work. I’d like you to discuss whether the office still has a role. Let’s start with you, Daniel.
Daniel: I think the office is still important, but not for the reasons managers usually give. It’s not about productivity—I’m actually more productive at home. It’s about learning. When I started my job, I learned most of what I know by overhearing people and asking quick questions. You can’t do that on a video call.
Tutor: So you’d say the office is mainly a learning environment?
Daniel: Yes, for junior staff especially. Though I accept that for experienced people it matters less.
Tutor: Maria, do you agree?
Maria: Partly. I agree that learning is a real issue, but I’d push back on the idea that it’s mainly about junior staff. I’ve changed teams twice, and each time I learned a huge amount from informal conversations—and I’m not junior. So I think the office matters for everyone, but in a different way: it’s where you build trust.
Daniel: That’s a fair point. I hadn’t thought about trust.
Tutor: Let’s take that further. If the office is about trust and learning, what does that imply for how often people should come in?
Maria: Not necessarily more often. It implies that when people do come in, the time should be used deliberately. If you come in and sit on video calls all day, you’ve wasted the commute.
Daniel: I agree with that, but I’d add a caveat. Some people—caregivers, for example—can’t come in easily. If we make presence a condition of trust, we exclude them. So the office should be optional, but well designed.
Tutor: Daniel, you said earlier you’re more productive at home. Is that true for everyone?
Daniel: No, I should be careful. That’s true for me, in my job, which is mostly writing and analysis. For someone doing collaborative design, it might be the opposite. So I’d qualify it: remote work suits focused individual tasks.
Tutor: Good. That’s a useful distinction. Maria, you mentioned trust. How would you measure it?
Maria: That’s difficult. You can’t measure trust directly. But you can look at whether people ask each other for help, whether new staff stay, whether meetings are honest. I’d rather use those indicators than count days in the office.
Tutor: So, to summarise: you both accept that the office has a role, but you disagree about whether that role is mainly for junior staff or for everyone. And you agree that presence should not be treated as a proxy for commitment. Is that fair?
Daniel: Yes, that’s fair.
Maria: Yes, though I’d say we agree more than we disagree.
Tutor: That’s often the case. Thank you both.

Section 4: Academic Lecture

Lecturer: Today I want to talk about disagreement—specifically, why learning to disagree well is harder than it looks, and what research in education suggests we can do about it.

Let’s start with a common assumption. Many people assume that disagreement is a sign that something has gone wrong. In fact, disagreement is often a sign that something is going right: that people are engaged, that they are thinking independently, that they care enough to say what they think. The problem is not disagreement itself; it is the way we handle it.

One useful distinction is between disagreement about facts and disagreement about values. Factual disagreements can often be resolved by looking at evidence together. If two people disagree about whether a bridge can carry a certain weight, they can test it. Value disagreements are different. If two people disagree about whether the bridge should be built at all, no amount of engineering will settle the question, because what is at stake is a difference in priorities. A common mistake is to treat a value disagreement as if it were factual—to keep producing statistics when the real disagreement is about principles. Recognising the type of disagreement is the first step.

A second strategy is paraphrasing. Before responding to an argument, try to state it accurately in your own words. This has two effects. First, it slows the conversation down, which reduces the chance of a reactive reply. Second, it gives the other person a chance to correct you if you have misunderstood. Research on classroom discussion suggests that students who are taught to paraphrase before responding are more likely to change their minds when presented with good evidence—and also more likely to be listened to.

A third strategy is concession. Skilled arguers often concede a genuine point before pressing their own. For example: ‘You’re right that the cost is high; my concern is whether the alternative is affordable.’ Conceding does not weaken your case. It makes the remaining disagreement sharper and more credible, because it shows you are not simply rejecting everything.

Finally, institutions can design for disagreement. Structured formats—formal debates, mock trials, deliberative discussions with assigned roles—give students practice in arguing positions they may not hold. The aim is not to produce students who agree with everything, nor students who argue for the sake of it, but students who can hold a position firmly while remaining open to revision. That combination—conviction without rigidity—is, I would argue, the most valuable outcome of an education in disagreement.

So, to conclude: disagreement is not a problem to be managed but a skill to be developed. It can be taught, it can be practised, and it can be assessed—not by whether students agree, but by how well they disagree.

grammar.title: 转折、让步、同意与不同意；转述观点
grammar.explanation: 在英语中，表达转折常用 however、nevertheless、yet；让步常用 although、though、even though、while、despite、in spite of。同意可以说 I agree that…、That’s a fair point；部分同意可以说 I agree up to a point, but…、I’d push back on…；不同意可以说 I’m afraid I disagree、I don’t think that’s quite right。转述他人观点常用 Daniel argues that…、Maria concedes that… but adds that…、She points out that…。注意转述时人称和时态的变化。
grammar.example: I agree that learning is a real issue, but I’d push back on the idea that it’s mainly about junior staff.

answers: Although
questions.explanation: 此处需要表示让步的连词，Although 意为“虽然”，符合句意。
questions.evidence: Although the cost is high, the alternative may be even more expensive.

answers: Maria agrees that learning is a real issue, but she pushes back on the idea that it is mainly about junior staff.

options: Despite the evidence is clear, he refused to change his mind.

answers: Despite the clear evidence, he refused to change his mind.

Do you prefer to discuss disagreements face to face or in writing? Why?
How do you usually react when someone disagrees with you?
speaking.part2: Describe a time when you disagreed with someone but the discussion was productive. You should say: who you disagreed with; what the disagreement was about; how you handled it; and explain why you think the discussion was productive.
part3: Why do some people find it difficult to admit they are wrong?
How can schools teach students to disagree respectfully?
Do you think online discussions make disagreement better or worse?
Should managers encourage disagreement in the workplace? Why or why not?

transfer.writing: Some people believe that employees should be required to work from the office at least three days a week. Others believe that employees should be free to choose where they work. Discuss both views and give your own opinion. Write at least 250 words.
